item.title: How Moral Injury Worsens Burnout
item.description:
Burnout

How Moral Injury Worsens Burnout

Ethical issues at work can make you feel like you're pushing a boulder uphill.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Though moral injury and burnout are distinct phenomena, research suggests they are also intertwined.
  • Facing ethical issues at work can intensify feelings of burnout.
  • When work teams build an atmosphere of trust and openness, both burnout and moral injury start to recede.

As someone interested in both morality and human motivation, I’ve found myself thinking recently about the connections between burnout and moral injury. Burnout, as you may have experienced viscerally, is a state of profound exhaustion in which you feel depleted and unmotivated after being too stressed for too long.

Moral injury, meanwhile, often happens when you know the ethical thing to do in a given situation, but can’t do it because you lack resources or support. During the COVID pandemic, doctors and nurses were often unable to treat patients adequately because they ran out of supplies and hospital rooms. And at countless workplaces, people who witness colleagues fudging numbers or cooking the books keep silent, fearing they'll be ostracized if they speak up.

Source: MismibaTinasheMadando/Wikimedia Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain

While burnout and moral injury are distinct phenomena, research suggests that not only are they intertwined, but moral injury can actually make burnout worse. In one study, the more morally distressing situations people faced, the more emotional exhaustion they felt, which is a major component of burnout.

Studies like this pass the smell test. For most of us, it’s easy to think of times when witnessing wrongdoing or injustice made getting through the day feel like a struggle. If you feel morally compromised at work, even setting a healthy work pace that balances rest and engagement isn’t going to replenish your energy.

In a recent editorial, American Medical Association president Bobby Mukkamala argues that burnout and moral injury can’t be solved just on the individual level, by those who are already suffering. Instead, these issues call for systems-level solutions.

I couldn’t agree more, and the good news is that certain systemic changes can strike at the root of both problems. Organizational research suggests that when managers encourage an atmosphere of trust and openness within their teams, people can feel safe speaking up about both moral qualms and mental overload, and team members can solidify practices of helping each other through these challenges so that no one feels isolated or cut off from support.

While writing my book The Art of Pacing, I was lucky enough to observe this kind of culture incubating among Brown University surgeons-in-training. When people feel psychologically safe from the get-go—an atmosphere Brown program leaders have worked to foster—it's easier for them to pace themselves through satisfying, decades-long careers, rather than hitting a mental or moral wall and leaving their chosen work behind.

Copyright Elizabeth Svoboda. A version of this post appears in my newsletter.

item.title: A Flawed Study Shaped the Treatment of Childhood Depression
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

A Flawed Study Shaped the Treatment of Childhood Depression

Misinterpreted clinical trial biased pediatric psychotropic meds guidelines.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • One flawed study biased a meta-analysis affecting clinical guidance and prescribing practices.
  • Anecdotes may be persuasive, but sound medical decisions require transparent, reproducible clinical data.
  • Psychiatric meds are health technologies whose risks and benefits are tested for use with pediatric patients.
  • Science relies on our willingness to reanalyze data, correct errors, and reject false conclusions.
Source: Pixart image generator 10/2026

Can one bad apple spoil the entire bushel?

In science, a single flawed study can sometimes distort a larger body of evidence. A recent report, “Prozac use for childhood depression skewed by single flawed medical trial,” describes how one clinical trial may have influenced a major synthesis of research—and, in turn, prescribing practices for children with depression.(1)

Medication as Mental Health Technology

  1. Drugs are a form of technology: They are the result of translating scientific knowledge into practical tools for treating health problems. From plant extracts and chemical synthesis to recombinant DNA, monoclonal antibodies, gene splicing, and mRNA, medications are engineered, tested, and produced for broad use. This is the very definition of technology! A new molecule may eventually help treat depression or another disorder, but only after careful study, including controlled clinical trials.
  2. More than 100 psychotropic medications are on the market, and the list continues to grow. These drugs include antidepressants, anti-anxiety medications, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, stimulants, and anticonvulsants.
  3. Medication development depends on rigorous testing. Because people can respond differently to the same drug, patients may need to try more than one option to find the best balance of benefit and side effects. Clinicians need accurate, reliable clinical evidence to guide prescribing decisions.

In the recent review, a central question for researchers was: “How well does Prozac work for children with depression, compared with other treatments?” When many clinical trials point in the same direction, pediatricians and mental health professionals take notice. Whatever one’s view of medicating children for conditions such as attention-deficit disorders, anxiety, or depression, everyone should want prescribing decisions to rest on sound evidence. In this case, however, a single trial conducted in Iran with only 40 patients appeared to have had an outsized impact on the evaluation of using Prozac—fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)—to treat pediatric depression.

Here is what happened. A meta-analysis combined results from multiple studies on this question. Researchers included several clinical trials comparing Prozac with other treatments, but one study from Iran, published 20 years ago, produced unusually strong results and exerted a disproportionate effect on the overall analysis. That outlier shifted the findings in favor of Prozac, helping to shape the message that Prozac was especially effective and preferred for treating depressed children. The concern is not that this medication necessarily caused unusual harm or side effects, but that clinicians may have been misled and made treatment decisions using flawed evidence that was less conclusive than it looked.

What This Case Reveals About Science

This case highlights a broader truth about how science works and how research is used to validate treatments. Anecdotes can be compelling, but they are not the same as scientific evidence. Personal stories may raise important questions, yet they have not been tested through systematic methods. One data point does not establish a trend.

A familiar example is “vaccine hesitancy.” When public figures elevate anecdotal accounts over tested evidence, the result can be unnecessary illness. For example, when parents decline the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine due to unsupported claims linking the vaccine to autism, this frightens parents away from child vaccinations. Information shapes behavior, and this behavior affects the health of an entire community.

Psychology explains why such claims gain traction. Contrarians and independent-minded people may resist broad health mandates when they seem to override individual choices. Yet population health sometimes depends on widespread participation in behaviors—such as vaccination or masking during an outbreak—that reduce risks not only for individuals but also for those around them. Consider the difference between wearing a seat belt and wearing a mask. If one passenger chooses not to wear a seat belt, the consequences may fall primarily on that person. If one infected and contagious person chooses not to wear a mask, others may be exposed, and the illness spreads. Public health asks us to balance individual preferences with the collective risk.

It is easy to forget that the medicines are, in fact, technologies. Researchers also rely on technology to develop the drugs, recruit patients, conduct trials, and analyze results. Artificial intelligence may soon accelerate the design of new molecules and model virtual clinical trials. But no computational shortcut will replace careful procedures or critical thinking. Clinicians must carefully examine a drug treatment’s record of effectiveness and safety. Decisions that affect health cannot be driven by viral memes or anecdotal claims.

In this case, scientists identified the problem, reanalyzed the data, and widely shared the corrected results. Pediatric clinical guidance was revised, and the claim that Prozac is superior for childhood depression now appears less certain. This does not mean clinicians have been told to stop prescribing Prozac to children. Other options are available, but the larger lesson is that science is not about always being right; it is about being willing to look again for errors, and revise conclusions.

We can leave the broader debate about medicating children with depression for another time. For now, the essential point is that we must keep testing—not only new medicines, but also the assumptions that shape how we interpret the evidence. Science depends on our willingness to question our conclusions. This is how science corrects itself and thus serves us better.

item.title: Who Am I Minus My Spouse?
item.description:
Identity

Who Am I Minus My Spouse?

Personal Perspective: Finding myself is an unexpected challenge in widowhood.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Being widowed requires figuring out who you are in a changed life.
  • Being suddenly single feels vulnerable.
  • Even in ways life looks almost the same, it's different.
Source: Elisa Photography / Unsplash

Not that I ever gave any thought to being widowed before it happened, but if I had, I probably would not have understood to what extent it would involve figuring out who I am.

I still don’t know how to be out in this world without the cloak of marriage between me and me.

I’m just kind of stumbling around, figuring out what I do because it’s what we did and what we did because it was what I liked to do. What to keep from my past life, what to let go, what to add. I can’t be the person I was before Tom because that person was in her 20s. I’ve only ever been an adult side-by-side with Tom. Now, suddenly, I’m figuring out what I like to eat. (Back in the day it was bacon cheeseburgers all the time. Not so much now.) Where I like to go. Who I like to hang out with. What I want to watch or listen to. Music was life for Tom, so that's what we listened to any time the TV wasn't on. He was in charge of choosing, always respectful of where our tastes differed. Now I feel disloyal on the days I listen to talk radio instead.

Weirdest of all, I’m single. Do I want to stay that way or try to date? At my age? At the moment the thought does not appeal, but I sure feel exposed and vulnerable walking around all unattached. I feel—embarrassing to say this—invalidated. (I know, I know...that's not only wrong but also insulting to all the other single people in the world. But it's just how I feel about me. You all are great.) When Tom went, he took part of my identity with him.

The same but different

The social world in which Tom and I circulated has, to a great extent, dissipated. Mick Jagger notwithstanding, rock ‘n’ roll has a shelf life, and as my peers and I move through our 60s, we indulge in fewer loud, late nights. Musician friends have retired, moved away, passed away. So in some ways, life would be different even if Tom were still around.

But it would be different with Tom, meaning much of it would be the same. Comfy and well-worn. We’d go out to eat, hang with friends, see live music. We’d take road trips. Visit family. We’d sit on the couch after dinner and watch TV and Tom would fall asleep and I would be annoyed, but that was life and it was dear.

Now even the familiar is different. I live in the same house and sleep in the same bed, but there's a big empty space in both. I have coffee every morning but make it myself instead of having it brought to me in bed. (He was an early riser, I'm not.) I still eat dinner every night, but not at the same time and not the same kind of meals; they might not be the meat, starch, veggie Tom insisted on. Some nights they're just chips and salsa (starch and veggie). I still watch TV on the couch after dinner but now dogs sleep next to me.

I eat out and see live music a lot less often because if I don’t want to go alone, both require a level of proactivity I don’t always feel up to. It was a whole lot easier to just turn to Tom and make a suggestion than it is to figure out who to call, get in touch, hope they’re free and interested, make a plan, and follow through. And now, instead of just riding along on what Tom wants to do sometimes, I alone am responsible for keeping myself entertained. It's a lot of work and more than once I've done things I thought I would like but it turned out I didn't.

Staying social, going alone

I try to stay busy, saying yes to most invitations—it’s a couples’ world so I don’t get many—hoping to enjoy myself. I don’t always have fun, but I give it a shot. I go out alone with varying degrees of success, sometimes arriving arrive at an event and leaving immediately, other times sticking around but so awkwardly that I berate myself for days after, wishing Tom were around because just the fact that he loved me was enough to make feel like less of a loser. Sometimes the stars align and I have fun and don’t do anything cringe. This feels like an accomplishment.

Of course it’s not all bad. Fortunately, as an introvert, I’m good at being alone. This past summer I loaded up the dogs and drove to the Oregon coast, where we spent a month. I took long walks on the beach, read, painted, hiked, and watched old movies. Were Tom still alive this would have been impossible because he had a business to tend (my work is portable), so it was something new and wonderful just for me and my dogs. (My dogs, never ours. That feels strange in itself.) I was sometimes lonely but mostly content. I hope to do it again next year.

But now I’m back home, negotiating a life that resembles my old life, but is very different. I haven’t felt this awkward in my own skin since I was a teenager.

I spent most of my life in a we and now, suddenly, it’s just me.

Whoever that is.

item.title: The Patient Voice Was Invited Into the Room. Was It Heard?
item.description:
Health

The Patient Voice Was Invited Into the Room. Was It Heard?

Personal Perspective: What is lost when we fail to listen to patients.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Medicine saves lives, yet we don't seem to have become better at understanding what survival feels like.
  • A room full of heart experts left me wondering who is listening to the people living with heart disease.
  • They have time for the technology but can run out of time for the patient.

Something has been bothering me since I spoke at a cardiology conference this summer.

The invitation felt significant. As both a psychologist and someone whose life has depended on cardiology since infancy, I was honoured to be part of a symposium alongside several highly respected professors. I arrived feeling optimistic.

For most of my life, congenital heart disease was viewed largely through a biomedical lens. Survival was the priority. While this has begun to change, I left the conference wondering how far we have really come.

Looking for the Patient

Walking through the exhibition hall, I was struck by the advances in technology and clinical care. Yet as the day went on, I found myself thinking less about conditions and treatments and more about the people living through them.

One interaction stayed with me. Hoping to discuss patient experience, I approached a heart charity's stand. Staff appeared busy filming promotional content for social media. Perhaps I arrived at the wrong moment, but it felt symbolic: considerable attention devoted to communicating about patients, less directed toward listening to them.

The exhibition hall was unexpectedly triggering. Surrounded by equipment and technology, I was transported back to the hospitals of my childhood and had to step outside to ground myself. Yet these were not simply memories from a distant past. As someone who still lives with congenital heart disease and depends on ongoing specialist care, the world I was walking through was also part of my present and future.

Although I attended as a psychologist and researcher, I was also there as a patient. I have experienced recent setbacks in my cardiac health and am currently off work while trialling one of the medications discussed during the symposium.

A Child on the Bed

The other presentations focused on highly technical aspects of cardiac care. I was discussing the psychological experience of living with congenital heart disease and a lifetime of medical intervention. I spent longer than usual on my own story because I wanted the audience to see healthcare through the eyes of a child receiving it.

As I spoke, several people left. They may have had other commitments, but the moment stayed with me because it echoed a question that had been growing throughout the day: What happens when discussion turns from disease to lived experience?

Later, I described childhood pacemaker checks: lying dizzy and breathless on a hospital bed while clinicians learned to use emerging technology, gripping my mother's hand and counting holes in ceiling tiles. A small ripple of laughter spread through the audience. I suspect people were responding to how much technology has changed. Yet I found myself wondering whether we had taken away the same story. I was describing what it felt like to be the child on the bed.

The final troubling moment came at the end of the session. Several speakers had overrun, and there was no time for questions after my presentation. Perhaps it was simply unfortunate timing, yet I could not ignore the symbolism. The one presentation focused on lived experience was the one that never became a conversation.

Perhaps part of what stayed with me was the contrast with psychology conferences, where lived experience often sits at the centre of discussion. These topics usually generate deep engagement and reflection. Their relative absence on this occasion left me wondering whether healthcare still finds it easier to engage with what can be measured and treated than with what it feels like to live through those experiences.

Back in the Patient Role

On the train home, I found myself thinking about the child I once was and the many children I had known on cardiac wards over the years—the ones lying in hospital beds while adults discussed conditions, procedures, and outcomes over their heads.

This is not a criticism of individual clinicians, many of whom are passionate advocates for psychologically informed care. Rather, it left me reflecting on a wider culture within healthcare. Even among deeply caring professionals, it can sometimes feel easier to discuss disease than lived experience.

I was also struck by how little attention was paid to the psychological well-being of healthcare professionals themselves. There was little discussion of burnout, compassion fatigue, vicarious trauma, or moral injury, despite these being well-recognised occupational risks.

Modern medicine has become remarkably effective at helping people survive. Understanding survival, however, is not the same as understanding what survival feels like.

The Emotional Cost of Speaking Up

The day also forced me to confront something I often overlook: the personal cost of repeatedly turning my own medical history into a teaching tool.

For years, I have shared my story in the hope of helping healthcare become more psychologically informed. Yet congenital heart disease is not a chapter of my life that ended in childhood. It is a lifelong condition that continues to shape my health, identity, and future. As someone who still depends on specialist cardiac care, I am never speaking solely about the past.

Looking after my own mental health is not separate from that work. It is what allows me to continue doing it.

Psychologically Informed Healthcare: How Far Have We Really Come?

As someone who has lived with congenital heart disease my entire life, I know how much has changed. When I was a child, survival was often the only conversation. Today, we know far more about the psychological realities of living with lifelong conditions and the importance of supporting patients, families, and healthcare professionals.

The evidence is there, yet psychologically informed care can still feel confined to a dedicated session or token talk rather than something embedded throughout healthcare. Patient experience should not be an optional addition to discussions of treatment and outcomes. It should help shape them.

item.title: Finding the Tailwinds That Help Us Move Forward
item.description:
Resilience

Finding the Tailwinds That Help Us Move Forward

Noticing what is helping us can change the way we meet life's challenges.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • In life, there will naturally be headwinds pushing against us and tailwinds helping us move forward.
  • We can look across the eight realms of wellness to identify what is hindering and what is helping us.
  • Gratitude allows us to widen our perspective and appreciate what is working and supporting us today.

So often, our attention gravitates toward what is wrong, challenging, or missing. Yet when we focus solely on what is not working, we lose sight of the things that are helping us along.

I find it helpful to think about the headwinds and tailwinds moving through our lives.

Headwinds are the pressures, stressors, and challenges that push against us. They are the things coming at us, demanding our attention, threatening to knock us off course, or making it harder to move in the direction we want to go. Some are temporary, while others are part of circumstances we cannot quickly change. Tailwinds are the forces supporting us from behind and within. They include our strengths, skills, relationships, routines, experiences, and values that help us keep going. They may not remove the headwinds, but they can help us meet them with greater support and perspective.

In Stress Wisely, I explore wellness through eight interconnected dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, environmental, occupational, financial, and spiritual. Each offers a different lens through which we're able to notice what is hindering us, what is helping us, and where we might find room for growth.

Wellness is an ongoing process of understanding what we need, noticing what supports us, and making adjustments as our circumstances change. Perhaps we are not sleeping as well as we would like, feel disconnected from the people we care about, are carrying financial stress, or have lost touch with the activities that give our lives meaning. These concerns deserve our attention, and sometimes they call for change, additional support, or a closer look at what is possible within our circumstances. At the same time, my gentle invitation is to ask ourselves: What is already working for me here?

The Physical Realm

It is easy to focus on what our bodies are not able to do or what we wish we could change, but we can also appreciate what they help us experience and what we are doing to care for them. Perhaps a 30-minute walk every day helps you clear your mind, a consistent bedtime is allowing you to show up with better energy, or you've learned to recognize when you are running on empty and need to slow down. These everyday choices matter.

If you thought of your body as a vehicle carrying you through life, what is helping you take good care of it and keep it going?

The Emotional Realm

Emotional wellness is about learning to recognize our feelings and respond to them with greater understanding instead of ignoring them or expecting ourselves to push through them. One tailwind may be your growing ability to name what you are feeling. Maybe you give yourself 90 seconds to sit with an emotion and let it move through you, find comfort in a creative outlet, or reach out to a trusted person rather than carrying everything alone. These are ways of making room for our emotions as we navigate the hard parts.

What helps you process your feelings and meet yourself with a little more compassion?

The Intellectual Realm

We learn through curiosity, reflection, conversation, and experience. Each and every one of us has skills we've developed over time, mistakes we've learned from, and different perspectives we've opened ourselves up to that have broadened our thinking.

Thinking of a particular area in your life, what have you learned, figured out, or become more capable of doing?

The Social Realm

We are not meant to navigate life alone. A friend who checks in, a colleague who understands, or a community where we feel we belong can remind us we are supported and valued. We can also notice the strengths we bring to our relationships, such as being a good listener, a thoughtful encourager, or a practical problem-solver. Connection is about the support we receive, but it's also about the ways we contribute to one another.

Who helps you feel safe, seen, and supported? What do you bring to the relationships that matter to you?

The Environmental Realm

Our surroundings can influence how we feel and move through our days. We can't always change our environment, but we can notice the places that bring a little ease. Maybe it's a favourite park bench, a sunny spot by your living room window, or a calm corner where you can collect your thoughts. Creating and spending time in hope-filled havens that offer comfort and inspiration can make a difference.

Which places help you feel more settled, connected, or at ease?

The Occupational Realm

Our contributions extend beyond paid work to include caregiving, parenting, volunteering, and the many responsibilities that make up our days. When the demands feel relentless, we may overlook the care we bring to our work, the problems we have solved, or the difference we make in the lives of others. A tailwind might be recognizing a task you carry out that makes someone else's day easier, setting a boundary around email, asking for support, keeping a commitment that reflects your values, or celebrating the small wins.

Where do you find meaning in the work you get to do, and what helps you do it in a sustainable way?

The Financial Realm

When financial pressures are weighing on us, it can be hard to see what we're doing well and what is working for us. Recognizing what's helping us doesn't mean pretending those worries aren't real. Perhaps you have become more aware of your spending, started a conversation you've been avoiding, learned something about budgeting, or reached out to understand your options.

What is helping you feel more informed, supported, or prepared when it comes to your resources?

The Spiritual Realm

Spiritual wellness can be rooted in faith, and it can also be found in our values, sense of purpose, and connection to something larger than ourselves. Noticing the moments that remind us of what matters most can help us make choices that reflect it. Maybe it's spending time in nature, being of service, a prayer practice or familiar ritual, or making time for the people and causes you care about.

When do you feel most connected to what matters most to you?

Final Thoughts

We cannot always choose what life brings our way. Yet even when things feel difficult, we can widen our view so that what is hard is not the only thing we see.

This is where I believe gratitude is one of the mightiest forces we have for living well. It draws our attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed, helping us recognize what is sustaining us today and what we can carry forward into tomorrow.

item.title: Latest Analysis: Circumcision Boosts Men’s Sexual Function
item.description:
Sex

Latest Analysis: Circumcision Boosts Men’s Sexual Function

A recent study about circumcision's effects is unlikely to placate opponents.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Removing the foreskin removes some touch-sensitive nerves, but most are in the head (glans) of the penis.
  • Some studies of circumcision show sexual impairment, while others show none—or even sexual benefits.
  • A recent analysis of 15 rigorous studies shows that circumcision enhances men's sexual function.

Circumcision is controversial, sexually and psychologically.

It involves surgical removal of the foreskin, the skin that covers the head (glans) of the penis. The foreskin contains touch-sensitive nerves. By removing them, circumcision opponents insist that it must reduce the penis’ sexual sensitivity and impair men’s pleasure. On Reddit and other Internet forums, opponents have denounced circumcision as barbarous, unfair to male infants, and physically and psychologically harmful.

Supporters counter that the vast majority of erotically sensitive nerve endings are located in the glans, not the foreskin, and that the procedure does not compromise men’s sexual function or pleasure. Recently, Turkish researchers analyzed 15 studies of circumcision and found that far from impairing men sexually, it enhances men’s sexual function.

The Study

The investigators conducted a meta-analysis of 15 previously published studies. Meta-analysis is a standard statistical technique that allows the results of small studies to be combined as if they’d all been one large trial. Study size is important. The larger the study population, the more likely the results are to reflect reality. The 15 studies involved 14,737 men, a huge number that lends credibility to the findings. The meta-analysis showed that, compared with men with intact foreskins, those who were circumcised reported greater sexual satisfaction (p < 0.001), improved erection function (p = 0.002), less pain during intercourse (p = 0.03), and fewer orgasm difficulties (p = 0.01) (Karaahmet and Lalaeh, 2025).

The researchers evaluated 15 studies, but many more have been conducted. How did they select those 15? They used the World Health Organization’s (WHO) guidelines for grading research rigor and chose only the most credible studies, which is important. Many studies of circumcision’s sexual impact have been biased either for or against the procedure.

Studies Showing Sexual Impairment: Questionable

  • Portuguese researchers surveyed a group of adult men who got circumcised for medical reasons. Post-surgically, they all reported less pain on intercourse, but also experienced more erectile dysfunction (ED). However, many who reported sex problems were also diabetic, and diabetes often causes ED. Using statistical techniques to eliminate the impact of diabetes, the sexual difference between circumcised and intact men disappeared (Dias, 2014).
  • Michigan researchers used the Internet to solicit 300 men for an online survey—64 intact and 236 circumcised (192 as infants). The latter were 4.5 times more likely to report using erection drugs, suggesting that circumcision increases the risk of ED. However, the participants were self-selected. Circumcision opponents look for opportunities to bash the procedure, for example, by participating in surveys like this one. The WHO guidelines would flag this trial as based on a biased sample (Bollinger and Van Howe, 2011).
  • Belgian researchers conducted a similar online survey that drew responses from 1,059 intact and 310 circumcised men. The latter reported less sexual pleasure. Again, the participants were self-selected and judged their own sexual function subjectively (Bronselaer, 2013).

These reports don’t inspire much confidence.

African Studies Showing No Impairment: Also Questionable

Circumcision reduces the risk of AIDS (below). Several studies have involved before-and-after surveys of African men circumcised as adults to reduce AIDS risk:

  • Kenyan researchers surveyed the sexuality of 2,784 uncircumcised sexually active men, and then 1,391 got circumcised. The investigators resurveyed all 2,784 every six months for two years. Among those who got circumcised, 72 percent said their erotic sensitivity had increased (Krieger, 2008).
  • Researchers in Uganda conducted a similar trial involving 4,456 intact men, 2,210 of whom got circumcised. After two years, more than 98 percent of both groups said they felt “satisfied” or “very satisfied” with their sex lives (Kigozi, 2008).

But these studies are also problematic. When they were conducted, AIDS was epidemic in Africa, and many participants feared for their lives. Researchers reassured them that circumcision had no sexual downsides. Critics charged that circumcised subjects felt so relieved to have their AIDS risk reduced that they parroted back what the researchers had told them—that circumcision has no sexual impact.

The African studies look biased.

Using WHO guidelines, the authors of the new report excluded many studies, both pro and con, such as those just mentioned, and included only the most methodologically rigorous studies, which showed that circumcision causes no discernible sexual impairment.

Not Health, Faith

Worldwide, one-third of men are circumcised. Judaism and Islam require it, so in Israel and across the Muslim world, the practice is virtually universal. Circumcision is also popular in the U.S. and Asia, but less so in Europe, Latin America, and non-Muslim Africa.

Jews and Muslims have circumcised boys for centuries. During the 19th century, the practice spread to Christians who believed—mistakenly—that it prevented masturbation. Circumcision is not medically necessary, but it offers health benefits in several areas:

  • AIDS prevention. The foreskin can trap pathogens. World Health Organization studies have shown that circumcising African men reduced their AIDS risk by 60 percent.
  • Phimosis. This condition involves unusually tight foreskins that don’t retract during erection. It can make erections painful. The treatment is circumcision.
  • Urinary tract infection. Men’s UTI risk is lower than women’s, but compared with intact men, circumcised men face less risk.
  • Penile cancer. It’s rare, but intact men face increased risk.
  • Women's health. Women partners of circumcised men have lower rates of cervical cancer, herpes, trichomonas, chlamydia, bacterial vaginosis, and human papillomavirus infection (HPV, genital warts).

These findings have prompted some Jews and Muslims to claim their faiths were medically prescient and required circumcision for health reasons. But theologians of both religions insist that the practice has always been an act of faith, that its medical benefits, while welcome, are coincidental.

For the vast majority of men, the controversy over circumcision and sexual function is moot. They’re either circumcised or not, and if so, the vast majority have lived that way since infancy and have no way to compare their sexual sensitivity before and after the procedure.

If you’re intact and want to believe you have superior erotic sensitivity, you’re free to feel smug. But the weight of the evidence shows that circumcision does not impair sexual function, and that circumcised men have no reason to fear they’re missing out on erotic pleasure and satisfaction.

item.title: Eating Disorder Recovery in the Age of GLP-1s
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Eating Disorder Recovery in the Age of GLP-1s

How to protect your recovery when everyone around you is trying to lose weight.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • Hearing people praise appetite suppression can bring up old eating disorder thoughts.
  • GLP-1 conversations can make it harder to trust the hunger cues you worked to reclaim.
  • You can set boundaries around weight-loss talk without explaining your eating disorder history.
  • Feeling envy or wanting to lose weight doesn't mean you've lost the progress you've made in recovery.

You're planning your birthday dinner and text the group for restaurant ideas. One friend writes back that she's excited to celebrate but doesn't care where you go, since she probably won't eat much now that she's on Zepbound. Another suggests somewhere with "lighter options" because she started Wegovy. Someone else jokes that you can all split an appetizer.

You've worked hard to be able to sit down to a full meal and enjoy it. Now you're bracing to be the odd one out at your own birthday. You feel irritated and hurt. A couple of these friends know your history, and you can't understand how they can talk on the thread about their medications and how little they eat. Then you notice a voice you rarely hear anymore. Your eating disorder voice is back for a moment, bringing a twinge of envy and the thought that it's not fair. You remind yourself how dark that part of your life was and how much the illness took from you.

Source: Photo by Haberdoedas on Unsplash

Diet Talk in the Age of GLP-1s

Weight-loss medications have been around for decades. In an earlier post, I wrote about their history, including the amphetamine “rainbow pills” handed out at diet clinics in the 1960s and the fen-phen boom of the 1990s. The pattern has been remarkably familiar: A medication arrives with promises of making weight loss easier, enthusiasm grows, and widespread use eventually reveals risks or limitations that received less attention at first. By then, another medication may be on the horizon, offering renewed hope that the results will be different this time. Today, much of that enthusiasm surrounds GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

While weight-loss advertisements have appeared in magazines, on billboards, and on television for decades, what feels different about this wave is the degree of visibility and accessibility. Now, you can open Instagram to look at a friend's vacation pictures and find yourself watching a video about GLP-1 medications. Telehealth companies and med spas advertise directly to consumers, often offering prescriptions after a brief online intake. Even when you aren't looking for weight-loss information, you may find it filling your social media feeds.

At the same time, more conversations are treating body size as a medical issue. “Obesity” is now referred to as a chronic disease, with the classification still based on BMI, a calculation basd only on height and weight that doesn't measure an individual's health. This shift reinforces the assumption that people in larger bodies need medical treatment to lose weight. With GLP-1 medications in the spotlight, weight loss is often presented as something you're expected to pursue for your health. If you're in recovery from an eating disorder, these messages can be difficult to question, especially when they come from healthcare providers or are presented as responsible health decisions.

Hearing about these medications from people you know can be even more difficult. A friend mentions how little she eats now or a family member says they're relieved to stop thinking about food. They may have no idea how that sounds when you've worked so hard to eat enough and respond to hunger. These conversations can stir up old fears about weight gain or leave you questioning what you've learned from your eating disorder treatment providers, particularly when the people around you seem convinced that losing weight has improved their lives.

The Prescription for an Eating Disorder

People who take these medications often say they think less about food. They may mention forgetting meals or feeling full after a few bites. If you're in eating disorder recovery, this can sound very much like the way you once described your illness. It can be disorienting to hear the experience being discussed with relief and sometimes pride, even by those who were once concerned about your “diet” and weight loss.

Much of eating disorder recovery involves learning to notice even subtle signs of hunger and eat in response. This may take years to achieve after you've learned to ignore or distrust your body. A friend talking about hunger as a problem that medication has solved can bring back doubts about whether responding to hunger is really the right thing to do, or even necessary.

The popular idea of "food noise" adds to the strain. Those of us working in the eating disorder field are very familiar with this phenomenon because being consumed with thoughts about food is a natural response to deprivation, as documented in the Minnesota Starvation Experiment in the 1940s1. We also know that labeling food “bad” and treating it as off-limits contributes to this “food noise.” Calling those thoughts noise to be silenced echoes what the eating disorder always claimed: that wanting food is the problem and quieting the want is the cure.

Protecting Your Peace With Food and Your Body

In order to protect your eating disorder recovery, it's necessary to separate someone else's choice from your own. Their decision to take a medication says nothing about what your body needs. Your friend's prescription came out of a conversation about their body. Your recovery came from years of work on your own.

Weight-loss talk can start before you have time to think about how you want to respond. Having one sentence in your back pocket can make those moments easier: “I'm trying to focus less on my weight and pay more attention to my body. Can we talk about something else?” You do not owe the whole table your history. I would practice saying it aloud, since boundaries can be harder to find when you're caught off guard.

While it's impossible to completely shield yourself from GLP-1 weight-loss messaging unless you move to a deserted island, it's possible to limit how much of it you actually consume. On social media, you can mute or unfollow accounts that post injection updates and before-and-after photos. If lunch turns into a conversation about weight loss and you can't, or don't have the energy to, redirect it, give yourself permission to excuse yourself.

At home, you may not get a break from it. If your partner or parent is on a weight-loss medication, you might sit down to dinner and watch them push away a plate that's still half full. They may mention how little they can eat now. Even when they say nothing, you take it in while you're trying to stay with your own hunger and fullness and enjoy the meal, all of which you worked hard to reclaim from your eating disorder. That's why the conversation at home needs to be more direct. Ask them to keep dose talk and body commentary away from shared meals. I imagine most people who care about you want to help and haven't connected their experience to your recovery.

If you're working with an eating disorder therapist or dietitian, bring these encounters to them, including the envy. Feeling a pull toward appetite suppression, wanting to lose weight, or fearing weight gain doesn't mean you're relapsing. It is useful clinical information about where your recovery needs support, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. Your therapist or dietitian can help you sort through what came up and plan for the next shared meal.

Source: hoto by kimber/Unsplash

Back at the Table

You return to the group chat, and this time your eating disorder doesn't get to write the reply. You pick the restaurant you love and plan to order what you want. You tell the friends who know your history that all this weight-loss talk is hard for you, as you've worked too hard to find peace with food and your body, and ask them to leave it out when you're together. Either way, you get to sit at your own birthday dinner and eat a full meal.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Banning Social Media Won't Fix Teen Mental Health
item.description:
Social Media

Why Banning Social Media Won't Fix Teen Mental Health

Teens need safer platforms, not bans that cut off vital sources of support.

Posted October 15, 2026

Key points
  • When it comes to teen mental health, social media is a double-edged sword.
  • For Black, Brown, and LGBTQ+ teens, social media can be a mental health lifeline they can’t find offline.
  • Instead of bans, we need consumer protection laws that make everyone’s safety and well-being non-negotiable.
Source: Sixteen Miles Out/Unsplash

Imagine this. Nearly every teen in Teentown hangs out at the same place: the Teentown Pool. It’s the place to connect, meet new people, learn about parties, and unwind. There’s just one catch: There’s no lifeguard on duty. One exists, technically, but they’re not by the pool and respond to emergencies unreliably.

Despite this, management still encourages teens to swim as long as possible, even if they show signs of fatigue or hypothermia. Most swimmers are fine. But those who aren’t are told it's their own—or their family’s—responsibility to know when to get out of the pool, and to live with whatever anxiety, shame, or fear the experience leaves behind.

There’s another catch. The pool looks private, but it isn’t. Management films swimmers, profiles them, and sells their data to advertisers pushing products that may harm their health: diet supplements to teen girls with normal BMIs, steroids to teen boys. And though Teentown Pool is advertised as teen-safe, adults occasionally slip in, posing as teens, to engage in disturbing, even illegal behavior.

Teens do their best to manage these risks: reporting hazards, taking breaks, ignoring ads, and avoiding the creeps, but it’s unfair to ask them to do it alone. Even so, most teens keep coming back, because the alternative—missing out on where their friends are—carries its own weight. They’re stuck in a bind: Stay away from Teentown Pool and be isolated, or swim and constantly watch their backs.

Does this mean pools are inherently unsafe for teens? Should they be banned until age 16, granted entry only after their birthday? Or is the problem not with the pool, but rather with the management?

By now, you’ve probably guessed that I’m not talking about a community pool. The example is farcical, but it tracks the very real risks and trade-offs teens face on social media every day.

On Instagram, nearly half of teens report receiving unsafe content or unwanted messages within the past month, and those who do report feelings of discomfort, sadness, and fear. “It made me feel sad and insecure,” one 13-year-old boy reported in a 2025 survey conducted by Design It for Us. “I really wanted Instagram to remove that account. But I see that they are still up, victimizing individuals.” A 14-year-old girl added, “It made me afraid to be female and Asian. I did not feel safe.”

Additionally, despite claims that Instagram encourages teens not to overuse the platform, 65 percent of teens report that they haven’t received a single reminder to log off in the past six months. And harmful advertising is common: 41 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the U.K. have seen ads for prescription-only weight loss drugs, and Black teens are more than twice as likely as white teens to be targeted by skin-lightening ads (46 percent vs. 24 percent), in a country that has significantly stricter regulations than the U.S.

And yet the picture isn’t only negative. For many teens, especially Brown, Black, and queer young people, these platforms are often where they find community that’s harder to come by offline. LGBTQ+ teens are more than three times as likely to rate online spaces as “very kind and very safe” as compared to in-person spaces. Significantly more Black young people (77 percent) rate social media as important for connecting with others who share their mental health concerns than their white peers (53 percent). This is the real double bind: The same feed that exposes a teen to hate speech might also be the only place they feel seen.

These issues are not a problem inherent to the technology. They’re a problem manufactured by greed—the drive to maximize profits and shareholder equity regardless of the human cost. They reflect a series of deliberate design decisions to deprioritize solutions that would cost companies money but protect consumer well-being, such as stronger data privacy protections, more user control over algorithms, and active content moderation. Other industries, from pharmaceuticals to food to vehicles, have rarely addressed consumer safety issues voluntarily. It’s taken public protest and binding legislation to force their hand, none of which has destroyed these industries' profitability. The technology industry is no exception. Teens agree that social media companies should be doing more to protect their well-being, with a full 76 percent reporting that it would be helpful to have more active moderation and deletion of bullying and harassing posts.

So what should we, as caring adults advocating for young people in our own lives, be pushing for to keep teens safe? One commonly advanced solution is age-related bans or restrictions on social media use. While simple and intuitively appealing, bans don’t work, according to growing evidence. In Australia, more than 85 percent of teens circumvented the nationwide ban within months. Age-verification requirements also enable Big Tech to collect more, not less, intrusive personal data from users. Most importantly, bans don’t address the root of the problem—the fundamental mismanagement of online spaces. Harms associated with social media don’t disappear when young people turn 16 or even 18. Over half of 18- to 22-year-olds continue to report encountering racist, sexist, and homophobic content online, and 53 percent report that they feel like they can’t control their use or end up using social media for a longer amount of time than they wanted to.

There are also underappreciated harms associated with banning teens from social media, especially for Black, Brown, and queer teens for whom these platforms often function as vital sources of connection and support that aren’t readily available offline. Cutting off access doesn’t make the underlying platforms safer; it just removes a coping resource from teens who rely on it most, rather than offering the safety improvements companies have chosen not to make.

Instead of bans, we need to push policymakers for clear, enforceable consumer protection laws that make everyone’s safety and well-being non‑negotiable. We also need to push tech companies to partner with teens to redesign platforms to support mental health and publicly report on progress. People of all ages deserve safe spaces, both online and in person, to congregate, share ideas and interests, express themselves, and unwind. The public will is there. Now we need policymakers to put public good over private profit.
